articles.title: Too Broad to Be Found: The Niche Failure
articles.excerpt: Originally published on OKAIHub. A broad niche feels like a bigger market. In practice it removes every surface you need to reach people: you cannot name the community to post in, the sentence that ma…
articles.body: Originally published on OKAIHub . A broad niche feels like a bigger market. In practice it removes every surface you need to reach people: you cannot name the community to post in, the sentence that makes a reader recognise themselves, or the keyword a searcher would type. The product stays technically fine and commercially invisible. How the failure shows up You will notice it in the small moments. A launch thread gets polite replies but no signups. Ad copy cannot be written without words like 'streamline' and 'empower'. Someone asks what your tool does and you give three different answers depending on who is listening. Copy describes features, not a person doing a job. 'An AI writing assistant for teams' names nobody. Channels are chosen by guesswork.
articles.author: Aaron kuai

articles.title: We tracked 287 AI answers about AI-visibility tools. Here are the sources ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Claude actually cite
articles.excerpt: When someone asks ChatGPT or Gemini "what's the best tool for X?", the answer is built from a handful of websites. We wanted to see which ones, so we measured it on a real case: our own product, AIVis…
articles.body: When someone asks ChatGPT or Gemini "what's the best tool for X?", the answer is built from a handful of websites. We wanted to see which ones, so we measured it on a real case: our own product, AIVisib, a tool that tracks how brands appear in AI answers. This is one brand, one snapshot, and a small sample. Take it as a field note, not a study. What we measured We asked 24 realistic buyer questions to four assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude) in English, French and Arabic, and collected 287 answers. Then we looked at two things: who gets recommended, and which sources the assistants cite.
articles.author: AIVisib

articles.title: Code splitting and dynamic import() do not hide your JavaScript
articles.excerpt: A common piece of advice in code reviews is: "put the paid logic in a dynamic import() so it is not in the main bundle." Route-based splitting, React.lazy, and "load this only after checkout" feel lik…
articles.body: A common piece of advice in code reviews is: "put the paid logic in a dynamic import() so it is not in the main bundle." Route-based splitting, React.lazy , and "load this only after checkout" feel like they move the sensitive code out of reach. They do not. Code splitting is a loading and caching strategy. It decides when a file is fetched, not whether a determined reader can get it. This article is about what a split chunk actually hides, how people pull those chunks anyway, and what to protect instead. A split chunk is still a public file A typical paywall-shaped split looks like this: async function openExporter ( ) { if ( ! user . plan .

articles.title: SaltStack's 61,126 Matches Make Minion Trust a First-Order Inventory Problem
articles.excerpt: SaltStack's 61,126 Matches Make Minion Trust a First-Order Inventory Problem SaltStack uses a master and minion architecture to manage configuration, execute commands and collect data across a fleet.…
articles.body: SaltStack's 61,126 Matches Make Minion Trust a First-Order Inventory Problem SaltStack uses a master and minion architecture to manage configuration, execute commands and collect data across a fleet. The master accepts minion keys, and an accepted minion can receive commands from the master. That relationship gives the control plane significant authority over the managed hosts. ZoomEye count-only queries on 2026-11-18 returned 61,126 matches for app="SaltStack" and 633 for title="SaltStack" . The application count can include masters, minions, API services, documentation pages and deployments that use the product name in a banner. It is not a count of exposed masters and it does not prove that a minion key is accepted.

articles.title: I Showed My Coding Agent Its Own Bug. It Copied the Bug Twice.
articles.excerpt: A blind "try again" fixed the bug on the first extra attempt. Telling the model exactly what it got wrong did not help at all. My local model wrote a next-permutation function that failed 3 of 5 test…
articles.body: A blind "try again" fixed the bug on the first extra attempt. Telling the model exactly what it got wrong did not help at all. My local model wrote a next-permutation function that failed 3 of 5 test cases. I showed it the broken code, the exact inputs it got wrong, and what it returned versus what was expected, twice. Both times it sent back the identical broken function, character for character. A separate run where I gave the same model zero information beyond "that didn't work, try again" fixed the bug completely on the first attempt. I wrote this with AI assistance, and I fact-checked and edited every claim myself. That result is the opposite of what I expected going in.

articles.excerpt: Malware cocktail delivers cryptocurrency theft payloads and iOS exploits, among other things.
articles.body: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday. ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers.

articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
articles.excerpt: Voyager 1 just reached a light-day in space, but Voyager 2 won't do the same until 2035, due to speed choices made throughout their 50-year missions.
articles.body: Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer?

articles.title: Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?
articles.excerpt: The British company Foundational thinks its laser-reflecting tech can help humanity fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test.
articles.body: A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem. Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit. Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years. Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors.

articles.title: 'Neuromancer:' Release date, cast & everything we know about Apple TV's new cyberpunk series
articles.excerpt: Hack into our handy guide to this electrifying adaptation of William Gibson’s cult ‘80s novel.
articles.body: We're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's " Blade Runner 2099 " is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with " Neuromancer " blasting onto Apple TV. Based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures.
